overview: The Aónikenk are a southern Tehuelche people of Patagonia, associated especially with the steppe between the Santa Cruz River and the Strait of Magellan. Hunting, portable homes and later horse travel supported life across this landscape. Community organizations today use the name Aonekkenk and work to sustain their language, history and identity.

periods.title: Weaving and horse equipment
periods.summary: Historical accounts document weaving among some southern groups by the late eighteenth century. Research connects much of this production with riding equipment, while hide cloaks remained important.

periods.title: Trade with Punta Arenas
periods.summary: Around the middle of the nineteenth century, Aónikenk visitors exchanged animal products for provisions and manufactured goods at Punta Arenas.

periods.title: Sheep estates expand in Magallanes
periods.summary: Large estates increasingly occupied hunting country. Their expansion restricted movement and access to land, undermining the conditions that sustained mobile communities.

periods.title: Occupation permits and restricted land
periods.summary: Argentina reserved land for Indigenous families in Santa Cruz, beginning with Camusu Aike in 1898. These permissions did not provide the security of land titles.

periods.title: A language recovery project begins
periods.summary: A Tehuelche language initiative began within Santa Cruz’s intercultural bilingual education program, linking teaching with community memory and reflection.

periods.title: Surveying twentieth-century family sites
periods.summary: Archaeologists recorded buildings and glass scrapers at four sites associated with Tehuelche/Aónikenk-Mapuche families. Their study was published in 2020.

periods.title: Community representation
periods.summary: Tehuelche communities of Santa Cruz elected José Guillermo Bilbao and Myrta Susana Pocón to the Indigenous Participation Council.

periods.title: A foundation shares language and history
periods.summary: Wenai Sh E Pekk celebrated its launch in February 2025. Its activity record also describes talks on Aonekkenk culture and language in schools.

items.text: Guanacos and rheas supplied food and useful materials. Knowledge of hunting grounds helped families choose recurring camps, or aike. Travel initially took place on foot; horses later changed transport and hunting. These changes were adaptations within a continuing history, rather than evidence that a single way of life had lasted unchanged.

Portable toldos used wooden poles covered with guanaco hides, allowing shelter to be dismantled for a move. Hide cloaks called quillangos provided clothing and a surface for multicolored geometric designs. The museum’s educational account connects materials from hunted animals with both everyday protection and skilled decoration.

Around 1850, visits to Punta Arenas connected hunting households with a colonial trading center. Hides, guanaco meat, feathers and rhea eggs entered exchanges involving such goods as yerba mate, sugar, biscuits and beads. This was an economy involving travel and negotiation, not an isolated subsistence system.

Méndez’s study finds evidence of weaving among some Aónikenk groups before large sheep estates displaced them. She therefore questions the explanation that weaving began simply because hides became scarce. The dating rests on historical accounts, and the study does not claim every group adopted the practice simultaneously.

Woven bands and saddle coverings met needs created by horse riding. Hide cloaks continued to be worn, while some woven clothing came through trade. Méndez interprets this pattern as selective adoption: people chose particular uses for new techniques instead of replacing all their existing crafts.

The 2015 surveys at Rancho de Zapa, Vega Piaget, Hotel Punta del Lago and Laguna Puesto Peter recovered 94 glass scrapers. Most were fashioned from containers; one used window glass. Industrial seams on some pieces help place them in the twentieth century. The researchers connect this reuse of glass with hide working and trade.

At Vega Piaget, investigators recorded a timber-and-sheet-metal dwelling, a circular corral, water-management features and a garden area. These remains belong to the lives of Tehuelche/Aónikenk-Mapuche families in the twentieth century. They document settled rural work and changing building materials alongside craft practices, rather than a disappearance of Indigenous people.

sections.title: Loss of land and continued political life

items.text: Military campaigns and fenced ranches displaced families and cut across earlier stopping places. Between 1898 and 1927, collective occupation permissions designated several areas in Santa Cruz for Indigenous families. As Rodríguez and Horlent explain, these precarious permits differed from ownership, leaving families exposed to further encroachment and bureaucratic disputes.

The authors also describe Indigenous people traveling to Río Gallegos and Buenos Aires to defend assigned land. Such petitions and negotiations show continuing political action under unequal conditions. Neither incorporation into wage labor nor residence in a town erased community relationships or the history of dispossession.

In December 2018, the national Indigenous affairs agency reported the election of José Guillermo Bilbao, from Kopolke, and Myrta Susana Pocón, from Camusu Aike, to the Indigenous Participation Council. This dated record documents representation by living Tehuelche communities; it is not a statement about who holds those positions now.

The documentation project honoring Dora Manchado used shared activities to encourage conversation: looking at photographs, cooking, eating and visiting meaningful places. Its authors explain that these settings helped recover expressions and memories that formal questioning alone did not elicit. Some teaching dialogues were reconstructed collaboratively from shorter interactions, a distinction the project makes explicit.

Fundación Wenai Sh E Pekk describes work on a spoken dictionary, educational resources, talks and cultural activities. Its members identify themselves as children and grandchildren of language speakers. Their account puts community participation at the center of language recovery and directly challenges claims that the people belong only to the past.

The foundation records its public launch on 22 February 2025 and talks with pupils at primary school EPP No. 10 during the April Week of Indigenous Peoples. These activities bring language and history into contemporary education, alongside the preservation of older records and memories.

ending.text: Aónikenk/Tehuelche communities continue. Dispossession and restrictions on movement transformed their lives, but the map’s endpoint of 1500 is not a date of extinction. Present community organizations, language projects and public representation make that continuity explicit.
